Making six months of leadership coaching easier to picture.

Leadership coaching is personal, but the decision to book starts with practical questions. What would we work on? How long would it take? What does it cost? Waymark needed to answer those questions while giving founders a sense of Elin's approach.
The design challenge was to make an open-ended service feel tangible without reducing it to a rigid program or a list of promises.
I built the visual identity around a route: quiet greens, stacked stones and a line that moves through the site. The trail became a way to explain the work, rather than decoration around it.

A role picker starts with the visitor's situation—becoming a CEO, leading a larger team or making a difficult decision. From there, a six-month trail shows how the conversations develop. Three engagement options put the commitment and price alongside the work.
The About page introduces Elin as the person behind the service. On smaller screens, the same sequence becomes a clear vertical story, with the next step close to the information that supports it.

The finished site gives a founder enough context to decide whether a first conversation makes sense. They can explore their situation, understand the shape of the coaching and compare the options before reaching out.
The handover is a small Framer site with editable pages and a recognizable visual language that carries from the first headline to the booking decision.
Clear engagement options, with prices and commitments shown together.
“Ilse made the six months visible. The role picker starts with what a founder is facing, and the trail shows how we work through it. It sounds like my practice, not a coaching brochure.”

CallWave, AI phone answering for businesses

A business choosing an AI phone agent is handing over a first impression. A feature list cannot tell them whether the voice will sound right, handle an awkward request or know when to bring in a person.
CallWave needed a website that made those questions easy to explore, without asking visitors to book a sales call just to hear the product.

I put a playable conversation directly in the opening section. The interface pairs a voice waveform with plain descriptions of the task, so visitors can hear the product and understand what it is doing.

Six sample calls cover recognizable moments: booking, moving or canceling a visit, asking a question, reaching the team and calling after hours. A separate language section makes the voice choices tangible. Warm neutrals, green surfaces and an editorial typeface give the audio room to lead.

The setup section follows the decisions a business owner needs to make: add business details, set the agent's boundaries and test a conversation. Pricing comes after that explanation, with the differences between plans close to the price.
The website now works as a guided product demonstration. Visitors can listen to everyday calls, see where a person steps in and understand how they would configure the agent for their own business.
The design carries the same audio-led hierarchy onto mobile, where a visitor can try the product one conversation at a time.
Realistic call scenarios that explain the product by letting visitors hear it.

Turning an unfamiliar AI visibility service into a clear buying decision.

AI search visibility is difficult to explain because the thing a client wants—a useful recommendation—is several steps removed from the work an agency sells. Audits, citation work and tracking can all sound like interchangeable services.
Citebound needed to show what it examines, what it changes and what a client receives, without promising control over another company's AI answers.

I centered the site on the evidence an audit produces. Scorecards, source references and comparisons give the service a visible working language. The restrained black-and-white palette keeps that evidence readable; orange marks the decisions and next steps.

The services section separates diagnosis from ongoing work. The pricing page presents an audit, a citation program and a broader engagement as distinct commitments, each with its own scope. Case-study previews connect the offer to examples of the work rather than a wall of broad claims.

The audit form asks for the company, website, category and competitors before the request is submitted. It feels like the start of a useful brief, with the same visual vocabulary as the reports shown elsewhere.

The finished site gives a prospective client a route from an unfamiliar problem to a specific first engagement. They can inspect the report format, compare the scopes and provide a useful brief from one connected journey.
Its reusable report and case-study patterns give the agency a consistent way to present new work as the service develops.
An audit, a citation program and a broader partnership, each with a defined scope.
“Ilse gave us a way to show the work before explaining the category. The report examples, clear scopes and audit brief make the service feel concrete without promising an answer we can't control.”

A venture fund website that helps founders judge the fit.
For a founder, a fund's website is part of deciding whom to approach. Broad language about backing ambitious companies says little about the team's interests, experience or working style.
FirstCheck needed to make its investment focus and people visible, while giving portfolio companies a place of their own rather than treating them as a logo strip.

I gave the site a direct opening, supported by founder imagery and a clear invitation to pitch. The dark ground and compact typography keep the emphasis on people, companies and the fund's perspective.

The partner section states the investment range and areas of interest in a readable sentence. Individual profiles make the team easier to understand. Portfolio cards then bring each company forward with an image, a category and a short description.

Thought Pieces gives the fund room to explain how it sees the sectors it invests in. The portfolio, team and editorial pages use repeatable structures, so new companies and writing can join the site without redesigning the page.
The finished site gives a founder several ways to assess fit before sending a pitch: the stated focus, the companies already backed, the people involved and the team's writing.
Those parts share one visual system, with a mobile layout that keeps the pitch route close and the company stories readable.
Three ways for a founder to understand the fund before making an introduction.

Showing how a team's calendar can become its working surface.
Web design, product storytelling, Framer build

A calendar product has to earn its place beside tools people already know. Scheduling, planning, focus time and AI assistance can become a long list of features with no clear picture of a working day.
Nonlinear needed to explain how those pieces belong together and make the product interface the evidence for that explanation.
I led with the calendar itself. Product screens carry the story against a dark, quiet background, while the headings describe the job each screen helps someone do.

The feature section groups the product around planning, scheduling, focus and synchronization. Different calendar views show the same working context at different scales. The visual treatment follows the interface—small color accents, restrained borders and clear hierarchy—so the marketing page feels connected to the product.

Pricing makes the progression from an individual workspace to team coordination readable. The blog has topic filters and a repeatable editorial layout for product updates, practical advice and customer stories.
The finished site explains Nonlinear through a sequence a visitor can follow: recognize the calendar, see how the working modes connect and choose the level of coordination they need.
The interface stays visible on mobile rather than disappearing behind abstract illustrations, and the editorial system gives the team room to explain new features in context.
Plan, schedule, focus and sync, presented as parts of one workspace.
“Ilse organized the story around the way a week works. The screens do the explaining, and the page gives each feature a job. It feels connected to the product we are building.”

Making the boundary between an AI receptionist and a clinic team clear.
A clinic's calls range from routine booking to questions that need a person's judgment. A website for an AI receptionist has to explain that boundary as clearly as it explains the convenience.
Noted needed to show what a call sounds like, what the receptionist can handle and what the team receives when a conversation needs to be handed over.

I built the opening around four voices and the everyday tasks they represent. A larger sample-call section includes both straightforward requests and awkward moments, with transcripts and outcomes beside the audio.

The handoff section makes the limit explicit: a routine booking can continue, while an unapproved answer, a fee exception or a clinical question goes to the team. A reception note shows the caller's request, confirmed details and the action that remains.

Clinic-specific pages connect the shared system to situations a practice recognizes. A call-volume calculator makes pricing easier to explore, and the bright voice illustrations add personality while the rest of the layout stays calm and practical.

The finished site presents the service with its limits in view. A clinic can listen to representative calls, inspect a handoff and understand what its reception team still owns before booking a demonstration.
A shared layout supports different clinic types while leaving room for their appointment language, examples and imagery.
Routine requests and moments that need the clinic team, shown side by side.
